# Itunda Developers — Full Documentation

> Machine-readable developer documentation for building on Itunda.

## 1. Overview

Itunda Developers is the developer platform for building apps and integrations across the Itunda ecosystem.

Developer portal: https://developers.itunda.im/

The platform is organized around six capability areas:

- Apps — build modular Itunda experiences.
- Payments — integrate payment and transaction workflows.
- Business — connect merchants, customers, orders and commerce.
- Identity — build authenticated, user-authorized experiences.
- Place — build location-aware commerce and everyday experiences.
- Platform — shared developer tooling, environments and release workflows.

## 2. Developer journey

The recommended integration path is:

1. Choose a product capability.
2. Create credentials with the minimum required permissions.
3. Build locally where appropriate.
4. Test against sandbox-compatible flows.
5. Validate authentication, authorization and security boundaries.
6. Review the integration.
7. Request production access and launch.

Do not infer undocumented behavior from the rendered website. Prefer explicit API contracts and platform documentation.

## 3. Apps

Itunda Apps are modular experiences that can participate in the Itunda ecosystem.

Quick-start command:

    npx create-itunda-app my-app

The intended flow is:

    Create credentials
    → Run in sandbox
    → Test
    → Submit for launch

Keep an app's responsibilities within its documented product boundary. Do not assume access to internal Itunda services.

## 4. Payments

The documented developer entry point for payment integrations is:

    /v1/payments

Payment state is server-authoritative. Client-side state must never be treated as proof that a payment completed.

For sensitive money operations:

- authenticate the caller;
- authorize the requested operation;
- validate server-side state;
- use the documented device-verification requirements where applicable;
- do not place credentials or access tokens in client code;
- preserve request identifiers when diagnosing failures.

Only use request and response fields that are explicitly documented by the API contract.

## 5. Business

The documented developer entry point for business and merchant integrations is:

    /v1/business

Business integrations may connect merchants, customers, orders and commerce workflows.

Merchant authorization must be enforced server-side. Do not infer merchant privileges from UI state.

The Business website explains the platform. The separate Business App is the operational merchant experience.

## 6. Identity

The documented identity context entry point is:

    GET /v1/me

Example request shape:

    GET /v1/me
    Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
    Accept: application/json

The endpoint is authenticated. Keep access tokens server-side and request only the minimum permissions needed.

Identity data must be treated as user-authorized and server-authoritative.

## 7. Place

Itunda Place is the platform capability for location-aware commerce and everyday experiences in Rwanda.

Use only documented Place APIs and permissions. Do not invent endpoint paths, geographic identifiers, response fields or location behavior.

## 8. Authentication and credentials

Developer integrations use credentials and authenticated API access according to the documented product contract.

General rules:

- keep secrets server-side;
- never commit credentials;
- never put access tokens in browser bundles or mobile source;
- request minimum required permissions;
- validate authorization on the server;
- treat authentication and authorization as separate concerns.

A typical boundary is:

    Client
      ↓
    Itunda API
      ↓
    Authorized service

The client should not bypass the API boundary to reach internal services.

## 9. Environments

Use the appropriate environment for each stage:

### Local

Use for local development and integration work that does not require production resources.

### Sandbox

Use for safe integration testing before production access.

### Production

Production access follows the documented review and launch process. Do not assume sandbox credentials or permissions work in production.

## 10. API lifecycle

The current developer portal describes the public API surface as v1.

The intended lifecycle is:

    Documented contract
    → Sandbox
    → Integration test
    → Security/review
    → Production access
    → Launch

Treat documented contracts as stable boundaries. Do not build against inferred internal routes.

## 11. Errors

The developer portal currently documents these common API classes:

- 401 — unauthenticated.
- 403 — not permitted.
- 429 — rate limited.

For an error:

1. Read the documented error response.
2. Preserve the request ID or equivalent request-tracking identifier.
3. Fix authentication or authorization issues before retrying.
4. For 429 responses, use exponential backoff and avoid retry storms.
5. Do not blindly retry mutations.

Exact error fields and codes must come from the API contract; this document does not invent them.

## 12. Rate limits

The developer portal documents rate limiting as a first-class API concern.

When a request is rate limited:

- respect the documented limit;
- use exponential backoff;
- add jitter where appropriate;
- cap retries;
- avoid synchronized retry storms.

Do not invent numeric limits when the applicable API contract has not provided them.

## 13. Webhooks

Webhooks are intended for platform events delivered to an integration backend.

General handling:

1. Receive the documented event.
2. Validate the webhook according to the applicable contract.
3. Process it safely and idempotently.
4. Persist the necessary event/request identifier for troubleshooting.
5. Return the documented response.
6. Do not treat an incoming client-side signal as proof of a completed server operation.

Exact event names, payload fields and signature requirements must come from the applicable webhook contract.

## 14. Security

Security boundaries are part of the developer platform rather than an optional implementation detail.

Required practices:

- secrets stay server-side;
- access tokens stay server-side;
- use minimum permissions;
- enforce authorization server-side;
- treat payment and identity state as server-authoritative;
- preserve request IDs;
- do not expose internal services directly;
- do not bypass sandbox or review requirements.

Never place production credentials in source control, client bundles, screenshots or logs.

## 15. Observability and troubleshooting

When an integration fails, collect enough context to diagnose it safely:

- request ID or equivalent tracking identifier;
- endpoint and HTTP method;
- environment;
- sanitized server-side logs;
- relevant API error class;
- platform status.

Do not include secrets, access tokens, passwords or private user data in support requests or logs.

## 16. Launch checklist

Before requesting production launch:

- [ ] Credentials configured.
- [ ] Minimum permissions selected.
- [ ] Sandbox integration works.
- [ ] Authentication is implemented safely.
- [ ] Authorization is enforced server-side.
- [ ] Secrets are not present in client code.
- [ ] Payment and identity state comes from authoritative server responses.
- [ ] Rate-limit handling is safe.
- [ ] Webhook handling is safe and idempotent where required.
- [ ] Request identifiers are retained for troubleshooting.
- [ ] Integration has passed review requirements.
- [ ] Production access has been granted.

## 17. AI agent instructions

Use https://developers.itunda.im/llms.txt as the short resource map.

Use https://developers.itunda.im/agents.md for agent-specific safety instructions.

When working on an Itunda integration:

1. Identify the capability before coding.
2. Prefer documented contracts over inference.
3. Start in sandbox.
4. Never invent endpoints, fields, permissions or SDK behavior.
5. Keep secrets and access tokens server-side.
6. Treat payment and identity state as server-authoritative.
7. Preserve request identifiers.
8. Respect rate limits.
9. Do not perform undocumented production mutations.
10. Ask for clarification when the requested behavior is not represented by a documented contract.

## 18. Machine-readable resources

Short index:

    /llms.txt

Full documentation:

    /llms-full.txt

Agent instructions:

    /agents.md

The portal should add an OpenAPI document only when the complete public API contract can be generated from verified backend schemas. Do not fabricate an OpenAPI specification from marketing-page examples.

## 19. Scope and source of truth

This document describes the developer capabilities and safety boundaries currently exposed by the Itunda developer portal.

Where this document and a verified API specification differ, the verified API specification is the source of truth for exact paths, parameters, schemas, authentication requirements and response codes.

Undocumented internal services are not part of the public developer contract.
